title: AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.5: Rewrite Queries for Better Retrieval
html:
AIP-C01 Skill 1.5.5: Rewrite Queries for Better Retrieval

A hands-on lab with query expansion, query decomposition and a Step Functions query pipeline. Task 1.5, post 5 of 7.

[IMAGE: cover-1-5-5.png — alt: "Skill 1.5.5: Rewriting queries for better retrieval"]

AIP-C01 Hands-on Labs · Domain 1 · Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation · Post 5 of 7. Hands-on lab, about 30 minutes.

Customers don't write like policy documents. “my trimmer's busted after 10 days, can i get my cash back??” shares almost no words with “Garden equipment: returns are accepted within 14 days”. And “Can I return a drill after 2 months, and which blade fits the HT-650?” is two questions in one; a single search tends to find passages for one half and miss the other. Better indexes don't fix this. Fixing the query before searching does.

What AWS says

Skill 1.5.5: Develop sophisticated query handling systems to improve the retrieval effectiveness and result quality for FM augmentation (for example, by using Amazon Bedrock for query expansion, Lambda functions for query decomposition, Step Functions for query transformation).

What it means in plain words

  • Query expansion: a model rewrites the user's question into several search queries in the documents' own vocabulary; you search all of them and fuse the results.
  • Query decomposition: split a multi-part question into self-contained sub-questions, retrieve for each, then merge.
  • Query transformation with Step Functions: orchestrate those steps as a workflow with branches, parallel retrieval, retries and an audit trail.

[IMAGE: t1-5-5-techniques.png — alt: "Query handling techniques: expansion, decomposition, conversational rewrite, HyDE, routing, orchestration and built-in decomposition"]

What we're going to do

  1. Search an informal question and a two-part question as typed: the baseline.
  2. Expand the informal question with Amazon Nova 2 Lite and fuse the results.
  3. Decompose the two-part question, retrieve per part, merge, and answer with citations.
  4. Combine them: classify each question first, then expand or decompose.
  5. Optional: run the same pipeline as a Step Functions workflow.

What you'll learn

  • When to expand and when to decompose.
  • How to get reliable JSON (a list of queries) from a model with tool use.
  • Why classifying first saves cost.
  • How a Choice state and a Map state turn the pipeline into an auditable workflow.

What you'll need

  • Time and cost: about 30 minutes (plus 20 for the optional part), under US$0.05
  • Region: us-west-2
  • Access: Python 3.10+ with boto3; Amazon Nova 2 Lite through the US inference profile; Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Files: github.com/prasanth2006z/aip-c01-labs, folder domain-1/task-1.5/skill-1.5.5-query-handling, plus the shared folder

The lab

Step 1: Baseline

pip install boto3
python query_lab.py baseline

Both questions go straight into the hybrid search from the Skill 1.5.4 lab. For the informal one, the garden policy may not reach the top three. For the two-part one, the results lean towards one half: drill returns or blade parts, rarely both.

Step 2: Query expansion

python query_lab.py expand

expand() asks the model for three search queries in formal policy wording, using tool use with a JSON schema (as in Skill 1.3.3) so the output is always a list:

"Rewrite this customer question as 3 search queries for a retailer's policy
 documents. Use formal policy wording, include product category names ..."

Typical output: “Hedge trimmer return policy”, “Garden equipment return window refund”, “Refund for defective hedge trimmer”. The original question is kept as a fourth query. All four are searched and fused with reciprocal rank fusion. The garden policy should now come first.

Step 3: Query decomposition

python query_lab.py decompose

decompose() splits the question into one self-contained question per thing asked:

Can I return a drill after 2 months?
Which blade fits the HT-650?

Each is searched separately, the results are merged, and the model answers from the merged passages, citing their IDs. Now both halves are answered: drills fall under cordless power tools (90 days if registered), and the parts passage names the HT-650 blade.

Step 4: Classify first

python query_lab.py pipeline

Rewriting every question costs a model call and adds latency. The pipeline first asks the model whether a question is simple or compound, then expands simple ones and decomposes compound ones. In production you'd also skip rewriting entirely for clean, short questions.

Step 5 (optional): Step Functions

query_tools.py doubles as one Lambda function with several actions. query_pipeline.asl.json calls it from each state:

Classify  ->  SimpleOrCompound (Choice)  ->  Expand | Decompose
          ->  RetrieveEach (Map, up to 4 in parallel)  ->  MergeAndAnswer
  1. Zip query_tools.py, ../shared/search.py and ../shared/corpus.json at the zip's root. Create a Python Lambda function query-tools from it (handler query_tools.handler, timeout 60 seconds). Its role needs bedrock:InvokeModel on Nova 2 Lite (the inference profile and the underlying models) and Titan Text Embeddings V2.
  2. Create a Standard state machine from query_pipeline.asl.json, replacing ${QueryToolsArn} with the function's ARN.
  3. Start an execution with {"question": "Can I return a drill after 2 months, and which blade fits the HT-650?"} and follow it in the graph view.

The graph shows which branch ran, each sub-query retrieved in parallel, and every input and output. Failed steps retry on their own. That visibility is why Step Functions beats one long Lambda function when a pipeline has several model calls.

Other techniques worth knowing

  • Conversational rewrite: a follow-up like “and drills?” means nothing alone. Rewrite it with the chat history into a standalone question before searching.
  • HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings): have the model draft a plausible answer and search with that, since it looks more like the documents than the question does.
  • Routing: decide which index or source to search, or whether to search at all.
  • Built-in: Bedrock Knowledge Bases can decompose queries for you in RetrieveAndGenerate (the query decomposition setting in orchestration configuration), with no custom code.

Common pitfalls

  • Parsing a model's free-text list: use tool use with a schema so you always get JSON.
  • Expansion drifts off topic: keep the original question as one of the queries, and fuse rather than replace.
  • Lambda AccessDeniedException on Nova 2 Lite: cross-Region inference profiles need permission on the profile and on the model in each Region it routes to.
  • Rewriting every query: adds cost and latency. Classify or route first.

Clean up

If you did the optional part, delete the state machine, the query-tools function, their roles and their log groups. Nothing else to delete.

What to remember

  • User wording differs from the documents → query expansion with a Bedrock model; fuse the results.
  • Several things asked at once → query decomposition; retrieve per part, then merge.
  • Follow-up questions → rewrite with conversation history into a standalone query.
  • Branches, parallel retrieval, retries, audit → Step Functions (Choice + Map) calling Lambda.
  • Least custom code → Knowledge Bases' built-in query decomposition.

The exam scenarios for this skill are in post 7 of this task: Task 1.5 Exam Notes.
